units.text: INT. COUNTY COURTROOM 4 - DAY
Oak and old varnish.
A high bench, a jury box, a gallery of pews.
The flag hangs limp.
The air conditioner wheezes.
LEOCADIA FERRARA, 50s, defense attorney, in a gray suit with a silk scarf, stands at the lectern, one hand resting lightly on a stack of exhibits.
At the prosecution table, MALACHI GRANT, 40s, the DA, sits with his fingers steepled, watching her with the patience of a man who has watched many people fall.
Behind the bench, JUDGE OSTROWSKI, 60s, a heavy-lidded woman with half-moon glasses, rolls a pen between her fingers.
At the rail, BAILIFF FINN, 30s, stands with his arms behind his back, stoic as a pillar.
Your Honor, the defense calls its final witness.
units.name: LEOCADIA

units.text: Who would that be, Ms. Ferrara?
units.name: JUDGE OSTROWSKI

units.text: The defendant's mother.
units.name: LEOCADIA

units.text: Objection.
units.name: MALACHI

units.text: Basis?
units.name: JUDGE OSTROWSKI

units.text: She wasn't disclosed.
units.name: MALACHI

units.text: She's been on the list since March.
units.name: LEOCADIA

units.text: She was struck from the list in April.
units.name: MALACHI

units.text: By whom?
units.name: LEOCADIA

units.text: By your own office.
units.name: MALACHI

units.text: That's a clerical error.
units.name: LEOCADIA

units.text: It's a convenient one.
units.name: MALACHI

units.text: Judge Ostrowski sets down the pen.
She removes her glasses and rubs the bridge of her nose.
The courtroom holds still, the only sound the wheeze of the air conditioner.
Bailiff, bring the jury out.
units.name: JUDGE OSTROWSKI

units.text: Yes, Your Honor.
units.name: BAILIFF FINN

units.text: He opens the jury room door.
Twelve men and women file out one by one, wearing the glazed expressions of the three-week juror, and sit in the box.
A woman in the back row clutches her purse.
A man in the front picks at his thumbnail.
Leocadia waits until the last juror has settled.
Then she walks to the center of the room, past the lectern, past the exhibits, and stops directly before the jury box.

Ladies and gentlemen. The state has told you a story. It is a clean story. It has a beginning, a middle, and an end, and in that end, a man you have never met is guilty. I want to tell you a different one. It is not clean. It has loose threads and missing pages. It begins with a woman who sat in a hallway for six hours waiting to see her son, and it ends with a woman who sat in the same hallway for three weeks.
units.name: LEOCADIA

units.text: Your Honor, this is argument.
units.name: MALACHI

units.text: Sit down, Mr. Grant.
units.name: JUDGE OSTROWSKI

units.text: He sits.
His jaw is tight.
Leocadia does not turn.

I am not going to ask you to believe my client. I'm going to ask you to believe his mother, because she has no reason to lie that the evidence has not already given her. She has already lost him once. She cannot afford to lose him twice. And if, at the end of this trial, you cannot say beyond every doubt that the man at that table did what the state says he did, then it is not a verdict she is waiting for. It is a hallway.
units.name: LEOCADIA

units.text: She stops.
The silence in the room has changed from heavy to taut.
Judge Ostrowski lowers her pen.
Mr. Grant, your objection is overruled. Bailiff, bring in the witness.
units.name: JUDGE OSTROWSKI

units.text: Finn pulls open the double doors.
In the corridor beyond, a small figure in a faded blue dress stands with her hands clasped before her, waiting to be asked.
Malachi stands slowly, but he does not speak.
Leocadia nods to the figure in the doorway.
The woman steps forward, one pace at a time, down the long aisle, and the gallery turns as one to watch her come.
Madam, please state your name.
units.name: JUDGE OSTROWSKI

units.text: The woman takes her place.
She looks at the jury, then at her son, then at the DA, and breathes in, and the whole room breathes with her.
